title: Onprem Airgapped artifact delivery & GPU drivers deep dive
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Polaris through on-prem air-gapped artifact delivery, offline licensing workflow for GPU drivers, and runtime performance tradeoffs (KV cache, batching, quantization). Discussed artifact bundle delivery process, driver versions, licensing file exchange, and next steps to run a pilot benchmark in their secure airgap environment.
next_steps: Redwood to provide sealed artifact bundle tar and checksum via secure courier and upload instructions (Jamie)
Polaris to confirm GPU models + kernel versions and provide whitelist for USB courier (Ethan)
SE to share optimization checklist and suggested quantization profiles (Ravi)
action_items: Jamie Park; Send manifest + offline-license instructions; 2026-01-22
Ethan Liu; Share GPU inventory (driver/kernel) and internal compliance contact; 2026-01-23

Header:
Date: 2026-01-20
Start: 09:21 PST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Shah (Redwood SE), Maria Gomez (Polaris - Platform), Ethan Liu (Polaris - ML Infra), Sanjay Patel (Polaris - Security)
Links shared: redwood.com/secure/offline-install (doc), artifact-manifest.pdf (link), sample-benchmarks.xlsx (link)

Summary (auto): walkthrough of artifact delivery and offline license process; discuss GPU driver constraints and runtime perf knobs.

[00:00] Jamie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we know Polaris has a fairly strict airgap process so today Ravi and I will focus on artifact delivery, offline licensing, and some perf knobs — KV cache, batching, quant, that sort of thing.
[00:23] Maria: Thanks Jamie, yeah appreciate it. short context — we have A100s and some H100s in two colo sites, but everything is behind a physical airgap and there's an internal procurement process for any external bits.
[00:37] Ravi: Great, yeah so first high-level: for on-prem air-gapped we produce a sealed artifact bundle that contains the model blobs, the runtime, wheel packages, and a driver-compat matrix. We also include an offline license file that you drop into /etc/redwood/license (or a location you designate).
[00:56] Ethan: Quick Q, does the artifact include GPU drivers? our security team usually insists drivers come from our approved vendor and we sign them, not sure we'd accept third-party drivers.
[01:10] Jamie: Good question. We don't ship signed Nvidia drivers by default. For enterprise air-gap installs we provide the Redwood runtime and the driver wrapper. Customer provides the vendor-signed GPU driver binary (NVIDIA RPM or .run). We provide an installer shim that validates the vendor driver is present and then configures the runtime.
[01:31] Sanjay: So the flow is: you hand us a tar, we validate checksums, our policies verify the vendor-signed driver, and then we run your shim? Is there an HSM step for license unlocking?
[01:45] Ravi: Yes that's correct. The offline license is a signed blob; we support storing license keys in a KMS/HSM or a local TPM. The installer can be configured to fetch the license from an HSM via PKCS#11 interface. If you need, we can also provide a manual passphrase unlock for initial startup.
[02:05] Maria: Okay. On the perf side — our main concern is p99 latency for short chat-style requests (~256 tokens) and throughput for long-batch inferencing at night. How do you recommend we balance KV cache and batching?
[02:22] Ravi: Two knobs: KV cache and batching. KV cache (prefix caching of KV states) is big for latency on repeated context — if you have many interactive sessions with similar prefixes, enable long-lived KV caching. For throughput-heavy offline jobs, you'd disable aggressive cache retention and push larger batch sizes.
[02:41] Ethan: Any numbers we can expect? we need ballpark p50/p99 on our A100 80GB setup.
[02:50] Ravi: Ballpark, on an A100 80GB with FP16 model we typically see p50 ~60-80ms for 256 token interactive requests and p99 ~140-220ms depending on attention patterns. For throughput for batched 1024 token workloads, you can see 10-15k tokens/sec across a 4-GPU pool with the right batching. This varies by model and quant profile.
[03:15] Maria: That p99 seems a bit high for our SLAs. Is quantization effective for reducing p99?
[03:22] Ravi: Quant helps cost/perf but can slightly affect tail latency because INT8 kernels sometimes have different execution characteristics. Our recommended approach is FP16 or mixed bfloat16 for p99-sensitive interactive workloads. Use INT8 for high-throughput offline jobs where small accuracy delta is acceptable.
[03:42] Jamie: Also worth noting we have kernel selection logic in the runtime — it chooses the best kernel based on sequence length distribution, so short sequences will pick low-latency kernels.
[03:54] Ethan: On KV cache eviction — does the cache persist across service restarts? we have a scheduled weekly job that reprovisions nodes.
[04:02] Ravi: The cache is in-memory by default but we support checkpointing to local NVMe for warm restarts. In air-gapped installs you can use local NVMe to persist KV snapshots; restore time depends on snapshot size — typical warm restore for a few GB is ~20-30s.
[04:22] Sanjay: Any special kernel or kernel module dependencies? our infra team is on RHEL 8 with a locked kernel version (4.18).
[04:32] Ravi: We have a matrix. For recent runtimes we recommend kernel >=5.4 for the best driver compatibility, but we also support 4.18 via our compatibility shim for most Nvidia drivers. We will include exact kernel-driver combos in the manifest. That's why we asked for your kernel version as a pre-step.
[04:50] Maria: Can you walk through the artifact transfer method? our policy mandates physical media courier for executables.
[04:56] Jamie: Sure. Our standard airgap delivery: we generate a signed tar.gz (artifact bundle) + a manifest with SHA256 checksums. We coordinate a vetted courier to deliver an encrypted USB or external drive. On receipt you verify signatures and checksums. We also provide an alternate approach: MD5/sha verify over an internal transfer if you have a secure inbound USB process.
[05:20] Ethan: Do you support FIPS crypto for the signing?
[05:24] Ravi: Yes, we can sign using FIPS-compliant algorithms; we note that in the manifest. For HSM, we can provide signatures generated from our HSM or provide a signed license backed by your HSM if you want to sign the runtime yourself.
[05:40] Maria: Regarding driver versions — our security only approves vendor-signed NVIDIA 535.86 and kernel patch q. You mentioned fallback drivers for older kernels earlier?
[05:52] Ravi: Right, for older kernels we have a compatibility shim. But in practice it's better to run the vendor driver matching the kernel. For NVIDIA 535.x we support CUDA 12.x stacks. The runtime will detect the CUDA libs and choose appropriate kernels. Again, the installer validates and refuses to proceed if driver deps don't match unless you override.
[06:12] Sanjay: What about offline updates of the license? if we rotate keys quarterly, do we need a new courier each time?
[06:20] Jamie: You can rotate via a secure signed license blob that you upload via your internal SCM — no physical courier needed for license-only rotations if your internal change control allows. The initial artifact and driver still require physical delivery in your case, but license refreshes can be delivered via your secure internal artifact repository.
[06:40] Ethan: Let's talk about quantization specifics. do you provide INT8 calibration tools?
[06:47] Ravi: Yes, we provide an offline calibration harness that runs on a small sample dataset to produce quantization calibration tables. We include recommended calibration configs for common LLMs. The harness is in the artifact bundle and runs without network. Note: INT8 reduces memory and token compute but may show degraded tail latency for some ops — we recommend testing with your workload.
[07:12] Maria: Any special devops knobs for batching? we have a mix of tokens-per-request that vary wildly.
[07:18] Ravi: Runtime supports adaptive batching: small requests are coalesced into micro-batches up to a configured max latency budget (e.g., 50ms). You tune max_batch_size and max_enqueue_ms. For interactive workloads set max_enqueue_ms low (10-40ms) and rely on KV cache. For nightly throughput jobs set max_enqueue_ms high to increase batch sizes.
[07:40] Ethan: Is there a ready dashboard for per-token cost and p99 traces?
[07:45] Jamie: Yes Redwood Console (local control plane option for Private) ships with per-route token breakdowns, p50/p90/p99, and per-request traces you can export. For air-gapped sites we provide a bundled console container that runs locally and pushes metrics to your internal Prometheus/Grafana.
[08:02] Maria: Ok great. A couple of edge questions: 1) can we restrict which models run on which GPU type? 2) do you support MIG partitioning?
[08:11] Ravi: Yes to both. We have model-to-pool routing. Madagascar.. sorry, I mean model-to-pool policies that let you pin models to GPU pools. We support NVIDIA MIG on A100/H100; runtime will detect MIG instances and schedule accordingly, but note that throughput per GPU will be lower per MIG slice.
[08:32] Sanjay: For driver installation we need a signed RPM and an offline package repo. Can your installer consume an internal offline repo?
[08:39] Ravi: The installer can be pointed to a local RPM repo or accept a .run file. We can produce a script to create a local yum repo from the provided vendor RPMs and run the installation offline. We will include an example repo layout in the artifact manifest.
[08:58] Jamie: Cool — quick recap of what we'll deliver: sealed artifact tar.gz, manifest with checksums and driver compatibility matrix, offline license blob, calibration harness for quant, and a step-by-step install doc including the shim for vendor driver validation. We'll also include a sample config for KV cache and adaptive batching tuned for interactive vs throughput.
[09:20] Maria: Good. For the pilot run, we want to validate p99 on chat loads and run a 24-hour throughput job. Suggested timeline?
[09:27] Jamie: Week of Feb 2nd for pilot benchmark. Action items: we'll send manifest and offline-license instructions by Friday, Ethan share GPU/kernel inventory by Saturday, Ravi will share the optimization checklist and quant profiles.
[09:40] Ethan: Sounds good. One more minute — our procurement requires a short paper on the offline license lifecycle and revocation process. Can you send that?
[09:47] Jamie: Yes, we'll attach a short security brief that covers license revocation, HSM integration, and signed manifests.
[09:55] Sanjay: Thanks everyone.
[09:58] Jamie: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot slot.

End of recording.
